content:
A common Christian answer to Ramadan sets a month of fixed rules against the freedom of the Gospel. Its proof text is Mark 2:18 to 20, where Jesus (peace be upon him) is asked why his disciples do not fast, and answers that the wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is with them.[1]

The verse does not end there, and the Gospels say a good deal more about fasting. Jesus fasted, taught his followers how to fast, and told them that a time of fasting would come.

This article aims to provide context to that claim, insha'Allah, in five facts from the Gospels, the Hebrew Bible, the early church and the Quran, which says: "O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed to you as it was prescribed to those before you, that ye may (learn) self-restraint" (2:183).[2]

Matthew 4:2 says: "When he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was hungry afterward." Luke 4:2 adds that "he ate nothing in those days".[3]

The number has a history. Moses "was there with Yahweh forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread, nor drank water" when he received the tablets (Exodus 34:28), and Elijah walked forty days and nights to Horeb on the strength of one meal (1 Kings 19:8).[4] The Gospel places Jesus in the line of the prophets who fasted before God.

The fast in the wilderness has a different form from the Muslim fast, which runs each day "until the white thread of dawn appear to you distinct from its black thread", and then "till the night appears" (2:187).[2] The shared ground is the act itself, abstaining for God, by a prophet whom both books honour.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says "when you fast", and assumes that his hearers will. "When you fast, don't be like the hypocrites, with sad faces... But you, when you fast, anoint your head, and wash your face; so that you are not seen by men to be fasting, but by your Father who is in secret" (Matthew 6:16 to 18).[5]

The warning is aimed at fasting for show. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) gave the same warning: "Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, God has no need of his giving up his food and drink."[6]

Both teachers judge the fast by what it does to the one who keeps it. The Quran names that purpose in one word, taqwā, the self-restraint of 2:183.[2]

Here is the passage the claim leans on, in full: "Can the groomsmen fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they can't fast. But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then will they fast in that day" (Mark 2:19 to 20).[1]

The answer concerns the time for fasting, and it promises a time to come. The early church took it that way. The Didache, a manual of church order from about the year 100, tells Christians not to fast "with the hypocrites" on Mondays and Thursdays, and to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays.[7] In Acts 13:2 to 3 the church at Antioch fasts and prays before it sends out Barnabas and Saul.[8]

The first Christians, then, kept fixed weekly fast days. The "freedom" set against Ramadan has no support in their practice.

The Hebrew Bible ties fasting to mourning, repentance and prayer in a crisis, and its prophets judged it by justice. "Isn't this the fast that I have chosen: to release the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and that you break every yoke?" (Isaiah 58:6).[9]

Eliezer Diamond's study of fasting in rabbinic culture shows how widely the practice ran among the Jews of late antiquity, as a tool of piety and of petition.[10] Jesus' fast and his teaching on it belong to that world.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) met the same tradition in Medina. Finding the Jews fasting on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, the day God saved Moses, he said: "We are closer to Moses than you," and fasted it and told the Muslims to fast it.[11] The Quran's "as it was prescribed to those before you" is the same continuity, stated as law.

Ramadan is fixed by the Quran: a month, from dawn to sunset, with food, drink and marital relations set aside, and with days made up later by the sick and the traveller (2:183 to 187).[2]

Lent varies by church. For Latin Catholics in the United States, Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fasting, one full meal for those aged 18 to 59, and the Fridays of Lent are days of abstinence from meat from the age of 14.[12] The Orthodox keep the monastic rule: no meat after Meatfare Sunday, no eggs or dairy after Cheesefare Sunday, and on most weekdays no fish, wine or oil.[13] Many Protestant churches leave fasting to the believer.

Calling Lent the Christian Ramadan, then, misdescribes both. What they share is the purpose Jesus and the Prophet named: restraint, repentance and turning to God.

The bottom line

Jesus fasted forty days, taught his disciples to fast in secret, and said that they would fast once the bridegroom was taken from them. The first Christians kept two fast days a week. The picture of a Gospel set free from fixed fasting, held up against Ramadan, has the Gospel against it.

Muslims do not take the law of Ramadan from the wilderness fast. It comes from the Quran and the practice of the Prophet (peace be upon him). The Quran itself places that law in the line of "those before you", and the fasting of Jesus stands in that line. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Mark 2:18 to 22; Matthew 9:14 to 17; Luke 5:33 to 39 (World English Bible).
  2. Quran 2:183 to 187, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Matthew 4:1 to 11; Luke 4:1 to 13 (World English Bible).
  4. Exodus 34:28; 1 Kings 19:8 (World English Bible).
  5. Matthew 6:16 to 18 (World English Bible).
  6. Sahih al-Bukhari 1903, report of Abu Hurayra, in the Book of Fasting; our translation of the Arabic.
  7. Didache 8.1.
  8. Acts 13:2 to 3 (World English Bible).
  9. Isaiah 58:3 to 7; see also Zechariah 7:4 to 10 (World English Bible).
  10. Eliezer Diamond, Holy Men and Hunger Artists: Fasting and Asceticism in Rabbinic Culture (New York: Oxford University Press, 2004).
  11. Sahih al-Bukhari 2004 and 3943; Sahih Muslim 1130, report of Ibn ʿAbbās; the wording quoted is that of al-Bukhari 3943, in our translation.
  12. United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, "Fast & Abstinence", on the Lenten rules for Catholics in the United States.
  13. Orthodox Church in America, "Lenten Fasting", in The Orthodox Faith, vol. 2, Worship; and its outline "Fasting and Fast-free Seasons of the Church".
